strengths: Addresses a meaningful problem: selecting intervention scopes while adapting interventions to observed contexts. Figure 1 clearly illustrates why ignoring context or intervening on all controllable variables can be suboptimal.
The historical-UCB scope-selection criterion is a useful methodological idea, and the separation of scope-selection regret from within-scope action regret clarifies the learning problem.
Experiments use 110 random seeds with uncertainty estimates, include settings where baselines can attain the optimum, and provide useful context, noise, and BO-backend ablations.
weaknesses: The reduction from general mixed policies to the analyzed bandit model is not established. Definitions 1–2 permit a context variable to depend on an earlier intervention, whereas Appendix B.1 assumes all contexts are sampled from a fixed distribution before choosing the joint action. For example, intervening on A can change C, which a later intervention B observes. Additional restrictions or a sequential treatment are needed to justify guarantees against the stated mixed-policy optimum.

The central regret proof contains identifiable gaps. On page 27, the action loss f_i*(c)−f_i(x,c) is bounded by the range of f_i* across contexts; this is false even for the smooth GP f(x,c)=Zx, whose optimal value is constant across contexts. Furthermore, Equation (21) and the proof's conclusion use the worst-arm information gain through c(T), while Proposition 1 and Theorem 1 state the sharper averaged-information-gain bound without justification. These require correction before the guarantees can be accepted.

The empirical comparisons do not sufficiently isolate the contribution beyond existing POMPS characterization and contextual causal optimization. Functional Causal BO is discussed but not evaluated, and there is no comparison of the proposed selector against simpler selection rules operating over the same scopes. The experiments primarily involve only one or two candidate POMPSs.

The scalability claim is insufficiently supported. Scope enumeration is explicitly exponential, while the 86-variable example contains extensive redundancy and reduces to two small scopes. No enumeration-time, memory, or runtime measurements establish scalability as graph complexity or the number of candidate scopes grows.

The connection between theory and implementation needs clarification. The analysis assumes known GP kernels, independent Gaussian observation noise, compact domains, and UCB maximization. Experiments instead use HEBO with learned transformations, and several SCMs have unbounded Gaussian contexts. The stated guarantees therefore do not directly validate the evaluated implementation.

Reproducibility remains incomplete in the supplied manuscript: the claimed public implementation has no repository link, and experimental kernel, acquisition, and exploration-parameter settings are insufficiently specified. SCM equations also contain consequential inconsistencies, including the missing Cancer term in Appendix A.1.2's PSA equation and the self-referential C4 equation in Appendix A.3.
